title: te-comp: A Complete MLIR Compiler Generating Self-Contained C Inference Engines for MCUs
summary:
Deploying deep learning on microcontrollers (MCUs) requires fitting both the model weights and runtime activations within tens to hundreds of kilobytes of SRAM and Flash. Existing approaches either use an interpreter with a pre-written kernel library or combine a Python code generator with hand-written C kernels. This incurs dispatch overhead and requires framework dependencies. None produces self-contained, dependency-free C code specialized to a given model.
  In this paper, we present te-comp, the first complete MLIR-based compiler that takes a standard model in .tflite or .safetensors format and emits all C source files needed for deployment: the inference engine (kernels, weight arrays, memory layout) and the RTOS integration layer with zero runtime dependencies.
  On 10 MCUNet CNN benchmarks, te-comp outperforms MCUNet TinyEngine by using 38% less SRAM (up to 5.9$\times$) and 15% less Flash, while generating complete C code rather than linking a pre-written kernel library. To demonstrate, we use te-comp to compile an 8.3M-parameter GPT-Neo transformer (TinyStories-v2) and deploy it on a single-core Cortex-M7 at 160MHz. The full firmware uses 249KB of 512KB SRAM and 3.62MB of 4MB Flash and achieves approximately 1 token/s interactive text generation via Q4_0 weight quantization, a stateful int4 KV cache, and vocabulary pruning -- a capability no existing MCU inference framework supports.

title: Silent Degradation during Auto-Vectorization of bf16/fp16 on RISC-V Under LLVM
summary: Low-precision numeric types such as 8-bit integers, bfloat16, and half-precision floating point (fp16) are often used in AI inference workloads to reduce memory bandwidth, and RISC-V's openly specified Vector extension (RVV) is a natural target for compiling such workloads with auto-vectorization. This paper examines whether LLVM's RISC-V auto-vectorizer handles these narrow types equally well, using a multiply-accumulate loop written for fp32, int8, bf16, and fp16. Under a common baseline target (-march=rv64gcv), int8 and fp32 vectorize cleanly, while bf16 and fp16 degrade to increasingly scalar-heavy fallback code, with fp16 falling back to per-element software conversion calls, unless additional target-feature extensions (zvfbfmin/zvfbfwma, zvfhmin) are enabled. Under QEMU user-mode emulation, the baseline bf16 and fp16 kernels execute $17.0\times$ and $75.9\times$ as many dynamic instructions as their extension-enabled counterparts. Compiler diagnostics do report this degradation, but do not distinguish, in their wording, between a limitation that a compiler flag resolves entirely and one reflecting an inherent conversion cost, leaving no direct signal toward the fix. These results are supported by assembly-level instruction analysis, by direct inspection of LLVM's optimization remarks, and by dynamic instruction counts collected under emulation.

title: Handling JAX
summary: Languages that target hardware accelerators typically expose a restricted, first-order core without recursion or first-class functions, leaving programmers without a principled way to express computational effects. This paper presents a technique for compiling effect handlers to such a constrained target. We introduce a novel translation that statically eliminates effect handlers, and prove that it preserves both typing and semantics. Moreover, we address the challenges of integrating effect handlers with structured control flow, where continuations cannot be constructed statically. The calculus and all our results are fully mechanized in the Lean 4 proof assistant. Finally, we implement our design as a library for JAX, a Python domain-specific language for accelerator programming, and demonstrate its expressiveness through practical case studies.

title: Proving the Wrong Program: Miscompilations as a Threat to zkVM Guarantees
summary: A zero-knowledge virtual machine (zkVM) lets an untrusted prover convince a verifier that a program, typically Rust compiled to RISC-V, ran correctly. The proof covers the compiled binary, so a miscompilation can make a correct zkVM produce a valid proof of a computation that differs from the developer's source. We present the first empirical study of miscompilation as a threat to zkVM guarantees, on the production zkVMs SP1 and Jolt. We assemble 88 known rustc and LLVM miscompilations with Rust reproducers, using an LLM agent to recover Rust triggers for 60 of 124 LLVM bugs reported only as LLVM IR. Many of the bugs carry over to zkVMs: 48 of the 88 make a guest commit a wrong output on SP1 and 46 on Jolt, including the same 15 rustc bugs on both. Most bugs that do not reproduce never reach the faulty code on the zkVM's target, e.g. because they need an instruction-set extension. Existing guest programs are rarely affected by accident. Across 13 guests of 10 popular SP1 projects, the buggy and the fixed compiler produce byte-identical binaries in 447 of the 552 guest-bug pairs that build, and the other 105 have the same code or agree on every input we ran. An attacker who contributes code to a guest, however, can trigger these bugs on purpose. For about $40 per project, an LLM agent found patches that look like ordinary optimisations, preserve the behaviour of the guest's source, and expose a known bug in 12 of 366 project-bug pairs, across 11 of 20 projects. In four cases the guest commits a wrong output, including an Ethereum client that rejects a valid block, and in the other eight it fails on a valid input. Reviewing or formally verifying the zkVM or the guest's source cannot catch such a patch, because both are correct. zkVM projects should treat their compiler as part of their trusted base and track the known bugs of their toolchain.

title: Properly defining Erlang lists
summary: We define list types, distinguishing proper lists, which end in the empty list, from improper lists, which may end in any value. Both are encoded as recursive types of cons cells, implemented in etylizer. This work found one OTP compiler bug. We propose a one-line sound improvement to Dialyzer's list handling that finds six instances of dead code in the OTP code base. We compare BEAM VM type checkers and catalogue how other languages design lists and cons cells.

title: Linking as Evaluation: Correct Separate Compilation via First-Class Environments
summary:
Separate compilation is central to modular software: components are compiled independently and linked into an executable. Separate compilation is correct when a linked program behaves like the program formed by merging its sources. This property is less routine to prove than type soundness because it requires a formal account of linking.
  We present $λ_{\mathsf{SCE}}$, a simply typed calculus in which linking, modules, and environments are all first-class. Programmers control module linking through a link operator, which a type-directed elaboration translates into ordinary terms of a core calculus of first-class environments. The core calculus's existing evaluation rules then perform the linking: linking as evaluation. Linking independently compiled modules yields the same core term as elaborating their source link. Therefore, compilation and linking commute by construction. As a result, separate compilation correctness follows directly from the semantics preservation for both static and dynamic linking. All meta-theory is mechanized in Lean 4, and we implement a compiler to WebAssembly in OCaml.

title: Reasoning about Shared-Qubit Concurrency in Quantum Computing
summary: In this paper, we develop a semantic model for the parallel execution of quantum circuits, providing a formal foundation for studying shared-qubit concurrency in quantum computing. As in classical shared-memory concurrency, parallel quantum circuits may interfere with one another through operations on shared qubits. However, quantum entanglement and the noncommutativity of quantum operations introduce additional challenges for reasoning about their correctness. To address these challenges, we generalise the classical Owicki-Gries method to quantum computing at the level of quantum circuits. Our approach enables compositional reasoning about parallel quantum circuits by separating the verification of individual components from the analysis of interference between them. We formulate proof rules for establishing the correctness of parallel quantum circuits and prove their soundness with respect to the proposed semantic model.

title: Warpline: Binary-Level Tracing and Unified Evidence for Agentic GPU Kernel Optimization
summary: LLM agents are becoming GPU kernel engineers, but they still tune kernels without seeing where the time goes. Hardware profilers report how busy each unit was, not where each warp's time went; intra-kernel tracers can show it, but only with hand-placed probes and a recompilation that alters the very kernel being measured. We present Warpline, which gives agents this view automatically while leaving the kernel essentially unchanged. Warpline analyzes the binary to decide which events to record and inserts probes into the binary itself without recompilation or any manual step. It then aligns the trace with hardware profiling data on one unified timeline. Because it needs only the binary, it can regenerate this evidence for every new version of the kernel at whatever level the agent edits it (source, IR, or PTX), closing the optimization loop without human intervention. On NVIDIA B200, across 35 kernels in Triton, CuTe DSL, and CUDA C++, Warpline adds a median overhead of 1.2% and leaves a median 99.9% of executed instructions unchanged, whereas existing tracers have median overheads of 1.6% to 13.2% and leave only 4.6% to 32.7% unchanged. Warpline also traces closed-source kernels, which these tracers cannot. On 10 SOL-ExecBench problems, agents using Warpline spend less time and fewer model requests than a bare coding agent and NVIDIA's Kernel Design Agents (KDA), yet lead both after every round in geometric mean and reach a 7.69$\times$ geometric-mean speedup, against 6.94$\times$ and 6.13$\times$. Two case studies further demonstrate that Warpline reveals hidden bottlenecks and provides actionable optimization insights.

title: An Investigation on Numerical Bugs in GPU Programs Towards Automated Bug Detection
comment: Published in Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering (PACMSE), ISSTA 2025, associated with the 34th ACM SIGSOFT International Symposium on Software Testing and Analysis (ISSTA 2025)
summary: General-purpose graphics processing unit (GPU) computing has emerged as a leading parallel computing paradigm, offering significant performance gains in various domains such as scientific computing and deep learning. However, GPU programs are susceptible to numerical bugs, which can lead to incorrect results or crashes. These bugs are difficult to detect, debug, and fix due to their dependence on specific input values or types and the absence of reliable error-checking mechanisms and oracles. Additionally, the unique programming conventions of GPUs complicate identifying the root causes of bugs, while fixing them requires domain-specific knowledge of GPU computing and numerical libraries. Therefore, understanding the characteristics of GPU numerical bugs (GPU-NBs) is crucial for developing effective solutions. In this paper, we conduct a comprehensive study of GPU-NBs by analyzing 397 real-world bug samples from GitHub. We identify common root causes, symptoms, input patterns, test oracles that trigger these bugs and the strategies used to fix them. We also present GPU-NBDetect, a preliminary tool designed to detect numerical bugs across six distinct bug categories. GPU-NBDetect detected a total of 226 bugs across 186 mathematical functions in four libraries, with 60 of the bugs confirmed by developers. Our findings lay the groundwork for developing detection and prevention techniques for GPU-NBs and offer insights for building more effective debugging and auto-repair tool.
